P0001.title: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit/Open
P0001.summary: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure.

causes.text: Connector at the regulator loose, corroded or unplugged
Solenoid coil of the regulator open
Broken wire in the harness, e.g. chafing or rodent damage
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Engine cranks but does not start, or stalls (normally closed valve)
Loss of power or limp mode (normally open valve)

P0002.title: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0002.summary: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure.

causes.text: Regulator sticking or worn due to dirt, debris or water in the fuel
High resistance at connector or wiring causing wrong current
Low-pressure supply problem: clogged filter or air in the fuel
Rail pressure sensor reading wrong values

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P0003.title: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Low
P0003.summary: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure.

causes.text: Harness chafed through, short to ground
Shorted turns in the regulator coil (resistance too low)
Water or corrosion in the connector
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P0004.title: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit High
P0004.summary: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. causes.text: Short to battery voltage in the harness
Open coil or wire, reported as high with ground-side switching
Connector fault at the regulator
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode
Rough running or diesel knock possible

P0005.title: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P0005.summary: The fuel shutoff valve is a solenoid valve that opens or blocks the fuel supply. On diesel engines it is usually closed without current, so that the engine stops reliably when switched off.

causes.text: Wire or connector interrupted or corroded
Valve coil open
Fuse or relay in the valve supply faulty
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Engine cranks but does not start

P0006.title: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Low

P0008.title: Engine Position System Performance Bank 1
P0008.summary: The engine control module learns how far each camshaft of bank 1 is offset from the crankshaft and compares this with a reference. P0008 is set when both camshafts of this bank are shifted in the same direction beyond a threshold.

causes.text: Primary or timing chain stretched
Chain tensioner worn or loose
Timing drive fitted incorrectly after an engine repair
Crankshaft reluctor wheel slipped

symptoms: Timing chain rattle, especially at cold start
Loss of power or rough running
Often stored together with P0016 to P0019

P000A.title: A Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 1
P000A.summary: This monitor does not judge the end position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments.

causes.text: Oil too thick or too thin, sludged, or oil level low
Screen at the oil control valve partly clogged
Oil control valve sluggish
Cam phaser leaking internally or worn
Generally weak oil pressure, e.g. worn oil pump or bearings

P000B.title: B Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 1
P000B.summary: This monitor does not judge the end position of the exhaust camshaft on bank 1 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments.

P000E.title: Fuel Volume Regulator Control Exceeded Learning Limit
P000E.summary: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure.

causes.text: Fuel volume regulator worn or contaminated
High-pressure pump worn, delivering less
Low-pressure side: clogged filter, weak lift pump or air in the fuel
Not calibrated after pump or regulator replacement
Rail pressure sensor drifting

symptoms: Often hardly noticeable at first, later loss of power
Hard starting if rail pressure is wrong

P000F.title: Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Activated
P000F.summary: On common-rail diesel and some gasoline direct-injection systems a spring-loaded pressure relief valve protects the rail and injectors: if pressure rises too far, it opens and returns fuel to the tank, often holding a reduced pressure for limp-home operation. The control module recognises the opening from the rail pressure signal and stores P000F.

causes.text: Fuel volume regulator stuck open or without current, pump over-delivers
Rail pressure sensor reading wrong, control runs into overpressure
Pressure control valve faulty, where fitted
Fuel return line blocked or kinked
Relief valve itself leaking or fatigued

symptoms: Sudden loss of power or limp mode

P0010.title: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Circuit (Bank 1)
P0010.summary: The engine control module drives the oil control valve (a pulse-width modulated solenoid) of the variable valve timing on the intake camshaft on bank 1. It checks the electrical state of this output and sets the code when the circuit is open, or when the measured state does not match the command, for example because of a short.

causes.text: Solenoid coil of the oil control valve open or shorted
Connector corroded, loose or soaked with engine oil wicking through the valve
Wiring harness chafed through or broken
Supply voltage missing, e.g. blown fuse
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Less pulling power at low and medium engine speed

P0011.title: "A" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance (Bank 1)
P0011.summary: The engine control module compares the commanded position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 with the actual position it calculates from the camshaft and crankshaft sensors. This code is set when the camshaft sits further advanced than commanded for longer than a calibrated time, or, depending on the manufacturer, when the target is missed in either direction ("system performance").

causes.text: Oil level too low, oil sludged or wrong viscosity
Screen at the oil control valve clogged with debris
Oil control valve mechanically sticking
Cam phaser worn or its locking pin sticking
Timing chain worn or fitted incorrectly after a repair

symptoms: Rough or unstable idle, as valve overlap is too large
Rattling from the timing drive at cold start

P0012.title: "A" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Retarded (Bank 1)
P0012.summary: The engine control module compares the commanded position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 with the actual position from the camshaft and crankshaft sensors. This code is set when the camshaft stays further retarded than commanded for longer than a calibrated time.

causes.text: Oil pressure or oil level too low, oil worn out
Oil control valve sticking closed or its screen blocked
Cam phaser defective or seized in its rest position
Timing chain stretched or jumped a tooth
Wear debris in the oil circuit, e.g. from a thrust bearing

symptoms: Noticeably less torque and pulling power
Rattle from the timing drive if the chain is stretched

P0016.title: Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation (Bank 1 Sensor A)
P0016.summary: The engine control module checks whether the signal of the intake camshaft on bank 1 (sensor A) arrives at the expected crankshaft position, usually while the camshaft phaser is in its rest position. P0016 is set when the deviation stays outside a calibrated window.

causes.text: Timing chain stretched, or belt or chain jumped a tooth
Camshaft phaser stuck at an end stop, oil control valve or oil pressure faulty
Incorrect assembly after a belt or chain replacement
Camshaft or crankshaft sensor signal disturbed
Reluctor wheel on crankshaft or camshaft slipped

symptoms: Rough idle and loss of power
Chain rattle at cold start on chain-driven engines
Risk of valve damage on interference engines if the timing has jumped

P001A.title: A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P001A.summary: A camshaft profile actuator switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between two or more fixed cam profiles with different valve lift and duration, for example by shifting a cam piece axially or by locking rocker arms or tappets with oil pressure. Unlike a camshaft phaser it does not shift the timing continuously.

causes.text: Connector at the actuator corroded, oil-soaked or loose
Wire broken, e.g. at the valve cover
Actuator coil open
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Less power at high engine speed because the profile does not switch
Higher consumption or uneven part-load running, depending on the profile

P0026.title: Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P0026.summary: A solenoid valve routes engine oil to a valve control element on the intake side of bank 1. Depending on the manufacturer this is a valve lift changeover or a camshaft phaser.

Feedback oil pressure switch faulty or leaking (systems with switch)
Screen in front of the solenoid clogged, or solenoid sticking
Mechanical fault in the valve train, e.g. locking pin or phaser sticking
Contact resistance in wiring or connector

symptoms: Loss of power, no extra pull at higher engine speed
Rough idle possible if a phaser is affected

Output driver in the engine control module faulty

P003C.title: A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P003C.summary: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. Profile switching solenoid sticking or its screen clogged
Oil supply to the switching elements leaking or restricted, e.g. worn seals
Locking pin in tappet or rocker arm, or sliding cam piece, sticking
Consequence of a circuit fault of the same actuator

symptoms: Lack of power at higher engine speed
Reduced power mode on some vehicles

Contact resistance or corrosion at connector or pins
Replacement sensor with a different heater type fitted
Engine control module faulty

Readiness for the sensor heater stays incomplete

Output driver or software of the engine control module

P0065.title: Air Assisted Injector Control Range/Performance

Air hoses to the injectors leaking, disconnected or blocked
Air passages at the injectors coked
Air leak distorting idle control

P0069.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure - Barometric Pressure Correlation

MAP sensor hose blocked, kinked or leaking
Barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) faulty
5 V reference or connector faulty

P006A.title: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 1

Mass air flow sensor dirty or manifold pressure sensor faulty

P006B.title: MAP - Exhaust Pressure Correlation
P006B.summary: On engines with an exhaust pressure sensor, mostly turbocharged diesels, the control module checks whether manifold pressure and exhaust back pressure fit each other, for example with the engine stopped, when both should be at ambient pressure. P006B is set when they do not.

causes.text: Exhaust pressure sensor faulty or its hose sooted or blocked
Manifold pressure sensor faulty
EGR or turbocharger fault distorting pressures

P006C.title: MAP - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation
P006C.summary: On turbocharged or supercharged engines the control module compares manifold pressure with the pressure measured upstream of the throttle, for example at idle or with the throttle wide open, where the two must lie close together. P006C is set when the difference exceeds a threshold.

Boost or inlet pressure sensor faulty
Manifold pressure sensor faulty
Throttle body fault

P006D.title: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 1
P006D.summary: Without boost, for example with the engine stopped or at low load, the pressure sensor ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger must read about the same as the barometric pressure sensor. P006D is set when the difference is too large; some manufacturers compare against an estimated barometric value instead and run the check once per ignition cycle.

causes.text: Inlet pressure sensor faulty
Barometric pressure sensor or control module faulty
Wiring, connector or 5 V reference faulty

P006E.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Supply Voltage Circuit Low

Connector at the actuator corroded or loose
Internal short in the actuator
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or reduced power mode

P00B7.title: Engine Coolant Flow Low/Performance
P00B7.summary: When the engine is hot, the thermostat should be open and coolant should flow through the radiator. P00B7 is set when the engine coolant temperature is very high (above about 117 to 119 °C in documented cases) while the radiator side stays much colder, so too little coolant flows through the radiator.

causes.text: Thermostat stuck closed
Low coolant level or air in the cooling system
Coolant pump delivering too little (impeller, drive; known cases on some engines)
Radiator or hoses blocked
One of the temperature sensors reading wrong

symptoms: High engine temperature up to overheating

P00B8.title: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 2
P00B8.summary: On engines with two intake paths, the control module compares the manifold pressure of bank 2 with the measured or calculated air quantity of that bank. P00B8 is set when the two do not fit together; the code does not say which value is wrong.

causes.text: Air leak in the intake of bank 2
EGR valve dirty or sticking open
Manifold pressure sensor or air flow meter dirty or drifting
Wiring or connector faulty

P00B9.title: Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low. Low Ambient Temperature

causes.text: Wax separation from summer or insufficiently winterised diesel in frost
Fuel filter clogged or water in the filter frozen
Fuel filter heater faulty
Lift pump weak

symptoms: Jerking or loss of power after starting

P00BA.title: Low Fuel Pressure - Forced Limited Power
P00BA.summary: "Forced limited power" is a term for a protective strategy in which the engine control module deliberately limits engine power. Regulations require the check engine light to come on within seconds when such an emissions-relevant limp-home mode is active.

causes.text: Fuel filter clogged, suction-side leak or air in the system
Lift pump or high-pressure pump weak
Pressure regulator or relief valve leaking
Tank run empty
Pressure sensor faulty

symptoms: Marked loss of power, limp mode

P00BB.title: Fuel Injector Insufficient Flow - Forced Limited Power

causes.text: Injectors coked or worn (flow drift)

P00BC.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow A Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too Low

These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more.

causes.text: Air leak behind the meter or charge-air leak
Air flow meter dirty
Air filter or intake restricted
Wiring or connector faulty

P00BD.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow A Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too High

P00C0.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit
P00C0.summary: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines.

causes.text: Wiring or connector damaged by turbocharger heat
Valve coil open or shorted
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle

Regulator coil open or shorted (often built into the pump)
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P00CE.title: Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
P00CE.summary: After a long standstill (six hours in a documented case) all intake air temperature sensors, for example intake air, charge air cooler and manifold temperature, should read about the same. The control module compares them in pairs: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own plausibility code.

causes.text: One temperature sensor drifting without setting its own code
Uneven cooling, undetected preheater or strong sunshine
Shared ground or reference line disturbed, falsifying several sensors
Engine control module or software

P00CF.title: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Correlation
P00CF.summary: With the engine stopped or without boost, the boost pressure sensor A (between compressor and throttle) must read practically ambient pressure. This code is set when it deviates from the barometric pressure sensor by more than a threshold; the code does not say which of the two is wrong.

causes.text: Boost pressure sensor dirty, oil-coated or drifting
Barometric sensor drifting, also when inside the control module
Contact resistance at connector, ground or 5 V reference
Sensor port or hose leaking or blocked

symptoms: Reduced boost or limp mode possible

P00D0.title: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor B Correlation
P00D0.summary: With the engine stopped or without boost, the boost pressure sensor B (between compressor and throttle) must read practically ambient pressure. P00D1.title: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1

causes.text: Heating element aged, resistance increased
Corrosion or contact resistance at connector or harness of the heater circuit
Too low supply voltage at the sensor connector, e.g. poor ground
Diagnostic software (manufacturer updates exist for some vehicles)
Replacement sensor with a different heater

symptoms: Oxygen sensor heater readiness stays incomplete

P00D2.title: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 2

P00D5.title: HO2S Sensor Correlation Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 1 Sensor 2
P00D5.summary: During fuel cut-off on overrun the exhaust gas is pure air, so the oxygen sensors before and behind the catalytic converter must both report the same lean value. A documented method averages and normalises the signals of both sensors during fuel cut-off and sets the code when they differ by more than a limit; it runs once per drive cycle and needs several overrun phases.

causes.text: Upstream sensor aged or shifted
Downstream sensor aged or shifted
Air or exhaust leak between the sensors falsifying the lean signal
Retrofitted sensor with wrong characteristic, or software

P00D7.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Temperature Too High

causes.text: Valve energised for unusually long periods, e.g. due to boost control problems

Heat shield missing or exhaust leak near the turbocharger
Contact resistance or supply fault distorting the estimate

symptoms: Whistling or fluttering when lifting off the throttle

P00D8.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Temperature Too High

P00D9.title: Ambient Air Temperature Sensor Circuit B

causes.text: Sensor faulty (exposed to spray and stone chips)
Connector corroded or wiring damaged, often after front-end work
Module supplying the value over the data bus faulty
Control module faulty

symptoms: Wrong or missing outside temperature display

P00E3.summary: Some engines, mainly hybrids and fuel-saving designs, have an exhaust heat exchanger behind the catalytic converter that transfers exhaust heat into the coolant for faster warm-up of engine and cabin. A bypass valve sends the exhaust either through the heat exchanger or around it.

P00F2.summary: The humidity sensor measures the relative humidity of the intake air; on documented vehicles it is built into the mass air flow sensor or a combined sensor. The engine control module uses the value, for example, to correct torque and in emission models.

causes.text: Connector or wire interrupted
Sensor or combined air flow sensor faulty

P00F7.title: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 2
P00F7.summary: This is the bank 2 counterpart of the comparison between barometric pressure and the pressure ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger. At low air flow the inlet pressure sensor reads close to ambient pressure, minus the small loss across the air filter, so it must match the barometric reading.

causes.text: Inlet pressure sensor of bank 2 drifting or dirty
Air filter or intake of bank 2 clogged
Intake hose between air flow meter and turbocharger leaking or slipped off
Barometric sensor faulty

symptoms: Reduced power or boost limitation possible

P00F8.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P00F8.summary: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly at the compressor outlet. It is a separate code family from the boost pressure sensor, which usually measures the pressure just ahead of the throttle; engines use it where the pressure behind the compressor is needed in addition, for example to judge the pressure loss across the charge air cooler or to protect against compressor surge.

causes.text: Connector loose or not fully engaged, or sensor not seated properly
Wire interrupted, short to ground or 5 V reference missing
Leak at the sensor flange or seal
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode with boost limitation

P00F9.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Range/Performance
P00F9.summary: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly at the compressor outlet. P00FB.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High

causes.text: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded
Sensor faulty internally (oil mist, heat at compressor outlet)

P00FC.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
P00FC.summary: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value.

P00FD.title: Battery B State of Charge Performance
P00FD.summary: 'Battery B' here is not a hybrid high-voltage battery (those have codes from P0B27) but, in the only documented use by FCA/Stellantis, the 12 V auxiliary battery of the start-stop system. When the engine restarts automatically, a relay separates main and auxiliary battery so that the auxiliary one keeps the control units stable while the main battery cranks.

causes.text: Auxiliary battery discharged or aged
Loose or corroded positive or ground connections at either battery
150 A fuse or fuse array in the power distribution centre open or poorly contacting
Battery separation relay stuck
Main battery faulty

symptoms: Start-stop out of service, 'Service Start/Stop' message
'Service Shifter' message with electronic gear selector

P00FE.title: EVAP System Tank Vapor Line Restricted/Blocked
P00FE.summary: The evaporative emission system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister and later purges it into the engine. P00FE means the vapour path between tank and canister is restricted or blocked.

causes.text: Kinked, pinched or misrouted vapour line between tank and canister
Charcoal canister broken down, grains blocking lines or valves
Rollover or fill-limit valve at the tank stuck closed (e.g. after overfilling)
Purge valve or leak detection module faulty
Tank pressure sensor reading wrong

symptoms: Fuel nozzle clicks off early when refuelling
Hiss or vacuum when opening the fuel cap

P00FF.title: Body Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P00FF.summary: P00FF is an information code in the engine control module: the body control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks over the data bus for the check engine light. The engine module stores P00FF so that a generic OBD scanner can see why the MIL is on; the actual fault is stored in the body control module as B or U codes and must be read there.

causes.text: Emissions-relevant fault in the body control module or its sensors/actuators (own B/U codes)
Software or calibration fault in the body control module
Communication fault on the data bus
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light on without an engine fault
Other messages depending on the body module fault

P0100.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit
P0100.summary: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency.

causes.text: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open
Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics)
Supply fuse or relay failed
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Rough idle, hesitation, lack of power (substitute value)

P0101.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

Leaking or disconnected crankcase ventilation
Clogged or wrongly fitted air filter, modified intake
Aged sensor or poor contact in the wiring

symptoms: Check engine light on, often without driveability problems

Sensor electronics failed
Interference from harness routed near ignition coils, relays or motors
Water in the connector or on the element

symptoms: Substitute value mode, lack of power

P0104.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0104.summary: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency.

causes.text: Loose contact at the sensor connector (corrosion, spread terminals, broken latch)
Chafed or partly broken wire moved by the engine
Sensor electronics dropping out (temperature-dependent)
Poor ground or electrical interference

symptoms: Check engine light on, may go out again
Occasional hesitation, misfire-like stumble, flat spot

P0105.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit
P0105.summary: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.

causes.text: Connector or wiring to the sensor open, shorted or loose
MAP sensor faulty (oiled, failed internally, SENT status fault)
Sensor hose disconnected, vacuum or boost leak
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same circuit
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit (diesel)
Rough idle, hard starting, higher consumption (petrol)

P0106.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0106.summary: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.

causes.text: Vacuum leak at the intake manifold or boost leak (hose, clamp, charge air cooler)
Sensor oiled or sooted, port blocked (EGR soot), characteristic drifted
High resistance in signal, reference or ground wire
Comparison sensor wrong, or mechanical cause (dirty throttle, EGR stuck open)

symptoms: Higher consumption, black smoke possible on diesels
Loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines

P0107.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P0107.summary: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.

causes.text: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open
Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing)
5 V reference shorted by another faulty sensor on the same circuit
MAP sensor failed internally
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Hard starting, rough idle, stalling possible
Wrong mixture from substitute value, higher consumption
Loss of power or limp mode on turbo and diesel engines

P0108.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P0108.summary: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.

causes.text: Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
MAP sensor failed internally
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Rough idle, loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines

P0109.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P0109.summary: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal.

causes.text: Loose contact at the MAP connector, terminals spread or corroded
Chafed or broken wire that makes contact with engine movement
Sensor with internal dropouts
Ground problem or control module

symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)

P010A.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit
P010A.summary: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010A is the general circuit fault of sensor B: no usable signal at all, just like P0100 for sensor A.

causes.text: Connector or wiring of sensor B open
Sensor B faulty internally (broken element)
Supply of sensor B missing (fuse, relay)
Control module input faulty

P010B.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P010B.summary: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010B is the plausibility fault of sensor B: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit.

causes.text: Intake pipe on the sensor B side leaking or not seated
Sensor B element contaminated (oil, dust)
Air filter on that side clogged or wrongly fitted
Boost leak on that bank, or sensor/connector problem

P010C.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Low
P010C.summary: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010C means the signal of sensor B is below its electrical lower limit – the counterpart of P0102.

causes.text: Signal wire of sensor B open or grounded, connector corroded
Sensor B electronics failed
Supply or ground of sensor B faulty
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Lack of power, substitute value mode

P010D.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit High
P010D.summary: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010D means the signal of sensor B is above its electrical upper limit – the counterpart of P0103.

causes.text: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to voltage
Sensor B electronics failed
Interference from harness routing
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Substitute value mode, lack of power
Rich mixture and higher consumption possible

P010E.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P010E.summary: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010E covers brief dropouts or jumps in the signal of sensor B without a lasting low or high fault, the counterpart of P0104.

causes.text: Loose contact at the sensor B connector
Chafed or partly broken wire
Sensor B electronics dropping out
Poor ground or interference

symptoms: Check engine light on, may come and go

P010F.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A/B Correlation
P010F.summary: Engines with two intake paths have two mass air flow sensors, A and B. On a symmetrical V engine both sides should draw about the same amount of air, so the readings can be compared with each other.

causes.text: Air leak or loose intake pipe on one side
One of the two sensors contaminated or aged
Air filter on one side clogged or wrongly fitted
Turbocharger or boost problem on one bank
Contact resistance in connector or wiring

symptoms: Mixture codes for one bank (P0171/P0174) possible

P0110.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Bank 1
P0110.summary: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage.

causes.text: Connector or wiring to the sensor open or corroded
Sensor or mass air flow sensor with built-in temperature sensor faulty
Sensor supply or ground disturbed
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Reduced power or torque limitation on some systems
Otherwise usually inconspicuous; cold start may be slightly worse

P0111.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
P0111.summary: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage.

causes.text: Sensor drifting or stuck at one value (ageing, oil from crankcase ventilation)
Contact resistance at connector or wiring distorts the reading
Comparison sensor (coolant, IAT2, charge air cooler) wrong
Undetected preheater, heat soak or sensor mounted near a heat source

symptoms: Slightly changed idle, power or cold start possible
Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P0112.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low Bank 1
P0112.summary: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage.

causes.text: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed insulation)
Sensor shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Retarded ignition, reduced power or torque limit on some systems

P0113.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High Bank 1
P0113.summary: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage.

causes.text: Connector unplugged or loose, or wire broken
Sensor open internally
Sensor return (ground) wire open
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Slightly richer mixture and higher consumption possible

P0114.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic Bank 1
P0114.summary: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage.

causes.text: Loose contact at the connector (corrosion, weak terminal tension)
Partly broken wire that opens with engine movement
Sensor with internal contact problem
Electrical interference or ground fault

symptoms: Occasional brief stumble or rough idle possible

P0115.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
P0115.summary: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.

causes.text: Connector corroded or loose, terminal spread
Broken or chafed signal or ground wire
Sensor faulty internally (short, open, coolant inside)
Control module input or 5 V supply faulty

P0116.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance
P0116.summary: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.

causes.text: Sensor drifting and reading too warm (ageing, coolant ingress)
Corrosion or contact resistance in connector or wiring
Block heater or preheater not detected
Comparison sensor (intake air, ambient) wrong
Control module calibration

P0117.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low
P0117.summary: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.

causes.text: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing, pinched harness)
Sensor shorted internally or coolant inside the sensor
Moisture or coolant in the connector
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Hard cold start (no enrichment, engine reported hot)

P0118.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High
P0118.summary: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.

causes.text: Connector unplugged or corroded, contact open
Broken signal or sensor ground wire
Sensor open internally
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Rich mixture, higher consumption, possibly black smoke or fuel smell

P0119.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0119.summary: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control.

causes.text: Loose contact or corroded connector pins
Harness chafing that briefly grounds or opens with engine movement
Sensor with internal crack or contact fault
Air pockets at the sensor (poorly bled cooling system)

symptoms: Radiator fan switches on for no reason
Occasional rough running or idle fluctuation

P011A.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1/2 Correlation
P011A.summary: Some engines have two coolant temperature sensors that check each other. P011A is set when both are electrically fine but their readings differ more than a calibrated amount under conditions where they should agree.

causes.text: Clogged heater core or restricted coolant flow at sensor 2
One of the two sensors drifting
Air in the cooling system or low coolant level
Block heater use in frost
Contact resistance at one sensor

P011B.title: Engine Coolant Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation
P011B.summary: After a long standstill the coolant and the intake air should both have settled close to ambient temperature. P011B compares the two sensors at start-up and is set when they disagree without either sensor showing a circuit fault.

causes.text: Coolant temperature sensor stuck or drifting
Intake air temperature sensor drifting or heat-soaked
Undetected preheater or uneven cooling
Contact resistance at a sensor connector or ground
Control module software (false setting, update available)

symptoms: With a wrong coolant reading: poor cold start, higher consumption or odd fan behaviour
Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P011C.title: Charge Air Cooler Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation Bank 1
P011C.summary: On turbocharged engines a charge air cooler temperature sensor sits downstream of the compressor, usually after the charge air cooler, and intake air temperature sensor 1 sits upstream near the air filter. While driving they differ by design, because compression heats the air.

causes.text: Charge air cooler temperature sensor drifting, oily or stuck
Intake air temperature sensor 1 drifting
Contact resistance at connector or shared ground
Undetected preheating or uneven cooling (sun, residual heat)

symptoms: Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P011D.title: Charge Air Cooler Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation Bank 2
P011D.summary: This is the bank 2 counterpart of P011C and only exists on engines with two separate intake paths, each with its own charge air cooler temperature sensor and intake air temperature sensor – for example V engines with twin turbochargers and separate charge air coolers. After a long standstill both bank 2 sensors should read nearly the same; if they disagree at start-up, without either showing a circuit fault, P011D is set.

causes.text: Bank 2 charge air cooler temperature sensor drifting, oily or stuck
Bank 2 intake air temperature sensor drifting
Contact resistance at connector or ground
Undetected preheating or uneven cooling

symptoms: Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P011E.title: Engine Coolant Temperature 1 / Ambient Air Temperature Correlation
P011E.summary: After a long standstill, typically six to eight hours, the coolant should have cooled to roughly the outside air temperature measured by the ambient sensor in the bumper or mirror. P011E compares coolant temperature sensor 1 with the ambient sensor at start-up and is set when they differ beyond a calibrated limit and no preheater was detected.

causes.text: Coolant temperature sensor 1 drifting
Ambient temperature sensor drifting or affected by engine heat or sun
Preheater not detected
Contact resistance in one sensor's connector or wiring

P011F.title: Engine Coolant Temperature 2 / Ambient Air Temperature Correlation
P011F.summary: This is the counterpart of P011E for the second coolant temperature sensor and only exists on engines that have one – for example at the engine outlet, the radiator or in the heater circuit. After a long standstill sensor 2 should also read roughly the outside temperature; if it disagrees with the ambient sensor beyond a calibrated limit at start-up, P011F is set without saying which sensor is wrong.

causes.text: Coolant temperature sensor 2 drifting
Ambient temperature sensor faulty or influenced
Preheater or block heater
Contact resistance at sensor 2

P0120.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit
P0120.summary: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).

causes.text: Connector at the throttle body corroded or loose, broken wire
Sensor or throttle body with integrated sensor faulty
5 V reference disturbed (short on another sensor of the same circuit)
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles

P0121.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Range/Performance
P0121.summary: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).

causes.text: Carboned or mechanically sticking throttle plate
Worn potentiometer track (signal sticks or jumps)
Air leak or faulty MAF/MAP sensor (model comparison)
Contact resistance in signal or ground wire
Sensor or idle stop misadjusted (cable systems)

symptoms: Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Shift problems on automatics (wrong load signal)

P0122.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Low
P0122.summary: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).

causes.text: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
Connector at the throttle body loose or corroded
5 V reference missing (open, or shorted by another sensor)
Sensor or throttle body faulty
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Engine barely responds to the pedal or stalls at idle
High idle, A/C switched off (cable systems)

P0123.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit High
P0123.summary: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).

causes.text: Sensor ground (low reference) open or high-resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or 12 V
Sensor or throttle body faulty
Moisture or corrosion in the connector

symptoms: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Raised idle or delayed throttle response

P0124.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Intermittent
P0124.summary: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open).

causes.text: Loose contact in the connector (spread terminals, corrosion)
Chafed or partly broken wire in the harness
Worn potentiometer track (dropout at a certain position)
Sensor electronics faulty (SENT)

symptoms: Check engine light, possibly only intermittently
Limp mode that disappears after restart

P0125.title: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Closed Loop Fuel Control
P0125.summary: Closed-loop mixture control using the oxygen sensors is only released once the coolant has reached a minimum temperature. CARB requires that this happens within set times – from 2006 two minutes if the engine starts up to 8 °C below the release temperature, five minutes if 8–19 °C below.

causes.text: Thermostat stuck open (especially in cold weather)
Coolant sensor reading too cold or slow (drift, contact resistance)
Low coolant level or air at the sensor
Much idling or coasting in frost
Engine control module

symptoms: Engine warms up slowly, heater stays cold for a long time

P0126.title: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Stable Operation
P0126.summary: The generic title refers to a coolant temperature that is not reached for stable operation, i.e. for releasing further functions and diagnostics; how manufacturers implement it differs.

causes.text: Coolant sensor frozen or faulty (resistance does not change)
Thermostat stuck open or low coolant
Contact resistance in connector or wiring
Engine control module

symptoms: Engine and heater warm up slowly

P0127.title: Intake Air Temperature Too High
P0127.summary: P0127 is not a circuit fault but a functional check of the air path: the measured intake air temperature is too high for the operating state. The logic is documented for a Bosch EDC16 diesel (Saab 9-3): if the intake air exceeds 130 °C and does not fall below it within 45 s after the exhaust gas recirculation valve is closed, hot exhaust gas is evidently still entering or the sensor is wrong.

causes.text: EGR valve stuck open or not sealing (diesel)
EGR cooler clogged or bypass flap stuck in bypass
Charge air cooler dirty or airflow through it blocked
Sensor reading wrong, or hot engine-bay air drawn in (loose intake duct)

symptoms: Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit
Knock tendency and retarded ignition on petrol engines

P0128.title: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)
P0128.summary: After a cold start the thermostat stays closed so the engine warms up quickly. CARB requires the coolant to reach a temperature at most 11 °C below the thermostat's rated value within a set time.

causes.text: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early
Coolant sensor reading too low, or corrosion and resistance in its circuit
Low coolant level or air in the system
Radiator fan running constantly (relay stuck, wrong control)
Driving pattern or conditions (much idling, extreme cold, strong heating)

symptoms: Temperature gauge stays low or drops while driving
Heater does not get properly warm

P0129.title: Barometric Pressure Too Low
P0129.summary: The engine control module needs the ambient air pressure for mixture, altitude correction and boost limits. It comes either from a dedicated barometric sensor or from the MAP sensor, read at key-on with the engine stopped and updated at wide-open throttle.

causes.text: MAP or baro sensor reading too low (dirty, oiled, drifted)
High resistance or corrosion in signal wire or connector
Sensor port or hose blocked
Control module (baro sensor often built in) or software

symptoms: Rich mixture, higher consumption, rough idle

P012A.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P012A.summary: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors.

causes.text: Connector or wiring open, corroded or shorted
Sensor faulty (SENT sensor reports internal error)
Control module software (false setting)
Engine control module faulty

P012B.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P012B.summary: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors.

causes.text: Sensor oiled (crankcase vent often joins before the compressor) or drifted
Air filter heavily clogged or intake blocked or collapsed
Leak in the intake pipe between filter and compressor or at the sensor flange
High resistance in the wiring
Comparison sensor (MAP, baro, MAF) wrong or software

symptoms: Loss of power or boost limitation

P012C.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P012C.summary: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors.

causes.text: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open
Signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor failed internally
Control module software (false setting)
5 V reference shorted by another sensor

P012D.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P012D.summary: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors.

causes.text: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground open or connector corroded
Sensor faulty internally
Control module software (false setting)

symptoms: Reduced power or limp mode possible

P012E.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P012E.summary: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors.

causes.text: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector
Broken or chafed wire making intermittent contact
Sensor faulty internally (erratic output)
Control module or software

symptoms: Occasional power reduction or boost fluctuation

P012F.title: Engine Coolant Temperature / Engine Oil Temperature Correlation
P012F.summary: P012F compares the coolant temperature sensor with the engine oil temperature sensor. The documented user is Ford's Power Stroke diesel.

causes.text: Oil cooler (oil-to-coolant heat exchanger) clogged – oil much hotter than coolant
Engine module software (false setting, especially in cold weather)
Coolant or oil temperature sensor inaccurate, or its wiring faulty
Thermostat stuck open or low coolant
Block heater in use (only coolant preheated)

symptoms: Check engine light and/or wrench lamp (Ford)
Raised oil temperature with a clogged oil cooler
Often no driving symptoms when software is the cause

P0130.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0130.summary: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.

causes.text: Wiring or connector of the bank 1 upstream sensor damaged, corroded or wet
Oxygen sensor faulty internally
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or mixture fault (plausibility versions)
Wrong or aftermarket sensor type
Control module or sensor interface chip faulty

symptoms: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
Sensor and catalyst readiness not set

P0131.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0131.summary: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.

causes.text: Signal wire (or a wide-band sensor wire) shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on exhaust or gearbox
Sensor faulty or poisoned (permanently lean signal)
Large exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or misfires
Connector wet or corroded
Control module or interface chip faulty

symptoms: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0132.title: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0132.summary: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.

causes.text: Signal wire shorted to the heater supply or battery voltage (melted or chafed harness)
Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short)
Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire (GM reads its bias voltage)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Sensor contaminated by silicone, coolant or oil

symptoms: Higher consumption, possibly soot or fuel smell
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
Often with P0138 or heater codes

P0133.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0133.summary: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip.

causes.text: Aged, sooted or poisoned upstream sensor (oil, silicone, coolant, additives)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (manifold gasket, crack)
Sensor heater weak or intermittent (sensor too cold)
Mixture fault: air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor

P015E.title: Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Fuel Timing Control

Control module software
Injectors outside tolerance or unstable fuel pressure
Injector wiring or sensors faulty
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Possibly louder combustion noise or uneven running with unlearned injectors

P015F.title: Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Cylinder Balance Control

P015F, by its title, is set when this closed-loop control does not become active within the expected time after starting, for example because the crankshaft wheel has not been learned or the conditions are missing.

P0168.title: Fuel Temperature Too High
P0168.summary: P0168 is not a sensor fault but an operating condition, almost only on diesels: the fuel temperature sensor reports fuel hotter than a protective limit. The fuel heats up through the return flow from the high-pressure pump and injectors, especially with little fuel in the tank, at idle after full load, in hot weather or with a failed fuel cooler; one manufacturer patent names about 80 °C as the upper limit to protect seals, against a normal range of roughly 5–60 °C.

causes.text: Fuel cooler (air or water cooler in the return) dirty or faulty, coolant circuit disturbed
Very little fuel in the tank at high load or heat
Excessive return flow from worn high-pressure pump or injectors, or faulty overflow valve
Fuel temperature sensor drifting and reading too high
Engine overheating or overload (trailer, gradient)

symptoms: Loss of power, limp mode (reduced injection quantity)
Occurs in heat, at full load, with little fuel in the tank

P0169.title: Incorrect Fuel Composition
P0169.summary: According to its title, P0169 means the control module has detected a fuel composition outside what is expected – wrong fuel or an impermissible ethanol or water content – while the composition sensor itself works. None of the manufacturer OBD documents checked (GM, Ford) uses the code: GM reports water or conductive fuel via the ethanol sensor frequency as P2269, and Ford has had no composition sensor since 2000.

causes.text: Wrong fuel (E85 in a non-flex-fuel vehicle, ethanol content outside calibration)
Water or contamination in the fuel
Fuel composition sensor drifting (value in range but wrong)
Control module software

symptoms: Poor cold start, stumbling, loss of power

P016A.title: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control
P016A.summary: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal.

causes.text: Oxygen sensor heater not working (fuse, fuse holder, wiring, heater element)
Oxygen sensor sluggish or aged
Control module software (false setting)
Engine not warming up (thermostat open, coolant sensor)

symptoms: Often with oxygen sensor or heater codes

P016B.title: Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Rich
P016B.summary: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal.

causes.text: Fuel pressure too high / high-pressure pump or regulator fault (direct injection)
Leaking injectors
Purge valve open
Oxygen sensor or air flow/pressure sensor offset, control module software

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P016C.title: Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Lean

Wrongly learned adaptation / control module software
Air flow or pressure sensor reading low, injectors clogged

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Stalling when stopping or at idle

P016D.title: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control
P016D.summary: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority.

causes.text: Rail pressure sensor drifting (wrong slope)
Volume or pressure control valve sticking or worn
Unstable low-pressure supply (filter, lift pump, air in system)
Fuel leak or high injector return flow
Control module software

symptoms: Occasional power reduction or rough idle

P016E.title: Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too High
P016E.summary: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority.

causes.text: Rail pressure sensor or its contacts/wiring (corrosion) giving a falsely high signal
Pressure or volume control valve sticking (lets too much through)
Return line from control valve or rail blocked or kinked
Control module software or calibration

P016F.title: Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too Low
P016F.summary: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority.

causes.text: Weak low-pressure supply: lift/tank pump, pump control module, clogged filter
Connector or ground problems (corrosion, water) at pump module, low-pressure sensor or ground point
Pressure relief valve open or its control circuit interrupted
Worn high-pressure pump or internal leak
Engine control module software

symptoms: Hard starting, long cranking, stalling after start

P0176.title: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit
P0176.summary: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature.

P017A.title: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit

Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407.

P017F.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Module Air Filter Restricted
P017F.summary: Leak detection pump modules in the evaporative emission system (for example Bosch's DM-TL, used by VW, BMW, Porsche, Volvo, Mini, Land Rover and Kia/Hyundai) draw fresh air through their own filter, often mounted separately via a hose; at rest the charcoal canister is also vented through it. P017F means this filter is restricted – by dust, mud or water when fitted near a wheel arch.

Moisture or ice in filter or hose
Hose between filter and pump kinked or blocked
Pump module faulty (wrong reference)

symptoms: Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0180.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0180.summary: Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. causes.text: Wire or connector open or corroded
Sensor faulty
Control module reference or ground

symptoms: Substitute value; possibly starting problems in cold or hot conditions

The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead.

causes.text: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Sensor B shorted internally
Moisture or oil in the connector
Control module

symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)
Oil temperature warning or maximum reading possible

symptoms: Check engine light or only a stored code

P01BE.title: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Bank 2
P01BE.summary: The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. Many V engines connect both rails and use only one sensor (P0190–P0194); the only documented user of the bank 2 codes is GM's 5.5 litre LT6 (Corvette Z06 2023–2024) with a digital sensor per rail.

causes.text: Connector or harness of the bank 2 sensor corroded or wet
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor faulty
5 V reference or ground disturbed
Control module

Bank 2 rail pressure sensor faulty internally
Genuine pressure fault on bank 2 (pump, control valve)

P01C3.title: Fuel Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P01C3.summary: Fuel pressure sensor A is a fuel pressure sensor without 'rail' in its name and without a bank – unlike the rail pressure sensors P0190–P0194 and P01BE–P01C2; which sensor it is depends on the manufacturer. The only documented case is FCA, where sensor A is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line, read together with the fuel pump control module.

causes.text: Connector corroded or wet, wire open or shorted
Sensor faulty
5 V reference or ground disturbed
Fuel pump control module or engine module

symptoms: Hesitation or lack of power under load

P01C8.title: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low Bank 2
P01C8.summary: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1.

causes.text: High-pressure pump of bank 2 weak or worn
Volume control valve faulty or its control disturbed
Supply pressure too low (lift pump, filter)
Leak in the bank 2 high-pressure circuit

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P01C9.title: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too High Bank 2
P01C9.summary: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1.

causes.text: Volume control valve not controlled properly (e.g. at low supply voltage), software
Volume control valve sticking
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor reading too high
Pressure relief path blocked

symptoms: Noise from the bank 2 high-pressure pump

P01CA.title: Fuel Rail Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking Bank 2
P01CA.summary: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1.

causes.text: High-pressure pump of bank 2 or its drive weak
Low supply pressure at start (lift pump, check valve)
Leak or leaking injector on bank 2
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor or connector

P01CB.title: Cylinder 1 Injection Timing Performance - Over Retarded
P01CB.summary: Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor.

causes.text: Injector worn, coked or sticking (opens late, delivers too little)
False setting from software or vehicle vibration (e.g. off-road tyres)
Wrong injector correction code stored after an injector replacement
Boost leak or loose injector clamp
Contaminated fuel

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P01E3.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 3 Circuit
P01E3.summary: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold.

causes.text: Open circuit or loose contact at connector or wiring of sensor 3
Sensor open or shorted
Short to ground or voltage in the harness
Control module

symptoms: Coolant temperature or cooling fan behaviour possibly affected

Signal wire shorted to 5 V or 12 V
Control module

symptoms: Coolant temperature or cooling fan behaviour possibly affected

P01E7.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 3 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P01E7.summary: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold.

causes.text: Loose contact at connector or pins
Wire break in the harness (movement, vibration)
Sensor opening internally with temperature changes
Corrosion or moisture in the connector

P01E8.title: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open
P01E8.summary: Engine coolant heater A is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599).

causes.text: Control wire or connector to the heater or relay open
Heater element burnt out or relay coil open
Fuse in the load circuit blown
Control module output stage faulty

symptoms: Longer warm-up, cabin heat slower in winter

P01F0.title: Coolant Temperature Relapsed Below Diagnostic Monitoring Temperature
P01F0.summary: Since model years 2019–2021 CARB requires petrol engines to detect a thermostat fault not only during warm-up but also when the coolant, after reaching operating temperature, drops back below the temperature needed for other diagnostics. P01F0 is this check.

Coolant sensor drifting cold
Low coolant or air in the system

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P01F1.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 4

causes.text: Sensor 4 aged or poisoned
Wiring or connector open, high-resistance or corroded
Sensor heater failed
Control module

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set

No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2.

P01F8.title: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P01F8.summary: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater A through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature.

causes.text: Short or partial short in heater element A
Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector
Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated
Heater running without coolant (low level, air pocket)

symptoms: Check engine light or warning message (manufacturer-dependent)
Slow warm-up, little heat in cold weather

P01F9.title: Engine Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P01F9.summary: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater B – a second heater or heating stage – through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature.

Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector

P01FA.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P01FA.summary: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238.

causes.text: Connector or pins at sensor B loose or corroded
Harness damaged (5 V reference, signal, ground)
Sensor faulty
Engine module or 5 V supply disturbed

P0200.summary: P0200 is the injector circuit fault without a cylinder assignment. The large US manufacturers do not use it – GM and Ford report injector faults per cylinder (P0201 ff) or as faults of the shared injector supply (P062D/P062E, P2146 ff).

Driver stage in the engine module faulty
Ground fault of the module or power stage

symptoms: Engine does not start or shuts down

P0201.title: Cylinder 1 Injector A Circuit/Open

The engine module watches each injector output: GM flags an open circuit at an impedance of 200 kΩ or more – on direct injection and diesel engines in 10 of 20 or 5 of 10 samples and with the warning light in the first trip, on some port-injected engines only after two trips.

causes.text: Connector at the cylinder 1 injector loose, corroded or with a broken or pushed-back pin
Injector coil open
Wire between module and injector open or chafed (heat, rodents)
Injector supply missing (fuse, relay) – then usually several cylinders at once
Driver stage in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Misfire and rough running, misfire code P0301
Limp mode possible on diesel and direct injection

P0213.summary: A cold start injector is an additional injector in the intake manifold that sprays extra fuel for a few seconds while a cold engine is cranked. In classic Bosch systems a thermo-time switch on the block powers it directly, without the engine module – such systems cannot set a code at all.

causes.text: Connector or wire corroded or open
Valve coil open or valve stuck
Thermo-time switch or control relay faulty
Driver stage in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Poor cold start, long cranking in cold weather
Leaking valve: hot-start problems, flooding, black smoke

P0214.title: Cold Start Injector 2
P0214.summary: A cold start injector is an additional injector in the intake manifold that sprays extra fuel for a few seconds while a cold engine is cranked.
