P05F8.title: Reductant Heater Control Module Performance
P05F8.summary: P05F8 is the function check of the DEF heater control module: its feedback does not match the command – heating current or power, temperature rise, or an internal module fault. The code is documented for Chrysler's 3.0 L EcoDiesel in the 2014 Ram 1500 and Jeep Grand Cherokee: several bulletins list it together with the heater codes P20BA, P20BE and P20C2, and the fix in each case was only reprogramming the engine module – a diagnostic that was too sensitive rather than a hardware defect.

causes.text: Engine module software (Chrysler 3.0 L 2014: diagnostic revised by reflash)
Heater control module faulty internally
Heater element or line in tank or hose with abnormal current
Unstable module supply or ground

symptoms: DEF warning in cold weather, possible heater codes P20BA/P20BE/P20C2

P05F9.title: Stop-Start Status Signal Circuit
P05F9.summary: A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB.

causes.text: Open status line or connector problem
Sending module without supply or faulty
Wrong software or variant coding (stop-start set without hardware)

symptoms: Stop-start indicator or message in the cluster
Check engine light only with some makers

P05FA.title: Stop-Start Status Signal Circuit Low
P05FA.summary: A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB.

causes.text: Status line shorted to ground
Sending module pulls the line to ground permanently (faulty output)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector

symptoms: Stop-start indicator or message in the cluster

P05FB.title: Stop-Start Status Signal Circuit High
P05FB.summary: A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB.

causes.text: Open status line or connector off
Sending module faulty or without ground
Short to voltage

symptoms: Stop-start indicator or message in the cluster

P05FC.title: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Performance Bank 2
P05FC.summary: During a cold start, direct injection petrol engines usually raise rail pressure for finer atomisation with multiple injections while the catalyst heats up. P05FC monitors whether the actual rail pressure of bank 2 stays within the target window during this phase – only engines with separate rails and pressure sensors per bank (V or boxer engines with two high-pressure circuits) can set it.

causes.text: High-pressure pump or volume control valve of bank 2 weak or sticking
Low supply pressure (low-pressure pump, filter)
Rail pressure sensor of bank 2 inaccurate
Engine module software
Leaking injector or pressure relief on bank 2

symptoms: Stumbling, hesitation or rough idle during warm-up

P05FD.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Temperature Too High
P05FD.summary: Electric variable-geometry turbo actuators use a DC motor with gearing, driven by an H-bridge in the engine module or in the actuator itself. Constant high load – sooted or stiff vanes, running against a stop, an internal motor short – drives up current and temperature.

causes.text: Vane mechanism sooted or stiff, actuator works constantly against resistance
Electric actuator faulty internally (shorted turns, bearing)
High ambient heat at the actuator (missing heat shield, exhaust leak)
Engine module or driver

symptoms: Loss of power or limp mode

P05FE.title: Active Grille Air Shutter C Performance/Stuck Off
P05FE.summary: Active grille shutters close the air inlet when little cooling is needed, to reduce drag and speed up warm-up. P05FE is the performance check of a third shutter C – target and actual position do not match, as P059F does for shutter A and P05AE for shutter B.

causes.text: Debris or ice blocking the louvres
Louvres unhooked or broken (impact)
Shutter C actuator faulty
Connector, wiring or supply corroded
Software false trigger in frost

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Higher coolant temperature under load or slower warm-up

P05FF.title: Brake Pressure Sensor/Brake Pedal Position Sensor Correlation
P05FF.summary: Stop-start decides when to stop and restart the engine from the brake: Ford stops it when the pedal switch is on and master cylinder pressure is high enough, and restarts when pressure falls below a filtered reference. P05FF means brake pressure (from the sensor in the ABS unit, sent over the network) and brake pedal position do not agree – for example pedal pressed without pressure build-up, or pressure without pedal.

causes.text: Brake pedal position sensor or switch misadjusted or faulty
Master cylinder pressure sensor in the ABS unit faulty
Network communication or software between ABS module and engine module
Air in the brake system or hydraulic fault (long pedal travel without pressure)

symptoms: No check engine light at Ford, possibly wrench or service warning
Possible related codes P0504 or brake pressure codes

P0600.title: Serial Communication Link
P0600.summary: P0600 means a serial data link that the module relies on has failed. At Ford it is the internal link between the main processor and the monitoring processor ('quizzer') of the electronic throttle safety concept: if data cannot be exchanged or check bytes are invalid, the code sets within about a second (diesel: 5 s), usually with the check engine and wrench lamps and a throttle failure mode such as an RPM limit.

causes.text: Internal module fault in the processor-to-processor link
Faulty module software (update available)
Open or short in a dedicated serial line between engine and transmission module (e.g. Subaru)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Fault in the transmission module at the other end of the line

symptoms: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or RPM limit (throttle failure mode)
Harsh shifts or transmission limp mode where the line links engine and gearbox
Other monitors such as the catalyst monitor do not run

P0601.title: Internal Control Module Memory Checksum Error
P0601.summary: The module continuously calculates a checksum over its program and calibration memory (flash) and compares it with the stored value; on newer units the flash error correction also reports bit errors it cannot repair. A mismatch means the stored software is corrupted.

causes.text: Interrupted or faulty reprogramming
Faulty module software (update available)
Defective flash memory in the module
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module

symptoms: Possibly no start or limp mode if the software is badly damaged
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected

P0602.title: Control Module Programming Error
P0602.summary: P0602 reports that the module is not, or not completely, programmed for this vehicle. GM checks at power-up and then every second whether a service replacement module still carries no calibration, and sets the code in the first trip; in brake modules a missing calibration set or a sensor ID that does not match also counts.

causes.text: Module replaced and not (completely) programmed
Programming interrupted by a voltage dip or lost connection
Wrong or incompatible software, calibration or configuration block
Internal memory defect in the module

symptoms: Check engine light or service lamp
Engine may not start or runs in limp mode
Appears right after a module replacement or software update

P0603.title: Internal Control Module Keep Alive Memory (KAM) Error
P0603.summary: Keep alive memory holds learned values – fuel trim, idle and shift adaptation, readiness status – while the engine is off, as long as the module has constant battery power; CARB defines it as memory that is lost when the battery or fuse is disconnected. The module stores a checksum of this memory at shutdown and compares it at the next start (Ford, GM Europe); GM calls the check 'long term memory reset', and the Ford diesel watches the supply of its engine-off timer chip (below 0.25 V).

causes.text: Battery disconnected, deeply discharged or replaced
Interrupted constant power feed to the module (fuse, wire, corrosion)
Main relay drops out too early, memory not saved completely at shutdown
Internal memory defect (EEPROM/NVM)

symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Rough idle or changed shifting until values are relearned

P0604.title: Internal Control Module Random Access Memory (RAM) Error
P0604.summary: P0604 means the module's working memory (RAM) failed its self-test: a value written to a cell does not read back correctly, a built-in hardware test fails, error correction reports faults, or protected memory is written without permission. GM's engine module scans the whole RAM within 30 s of start-up and then keeps checking in the background, setting the code after repeated failures with the lamp in the first trip; Ford tests RAM during initialisation, the GM gateway with error correction at start (two trips).

causes.text: Internal hardware defect of the module (RAM)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Faulty module software (update available)
Moisture or corrosion in the module or at its connector

symptoms: Limp mode or transmission limp mode
Several module codes at the same time

P0605.title: Internal Control Module Read Only Memory (ROM) Error
P0605.summary: P0605 reports an error in the module's program memory (ROM, today flash), found by a checksum or error-correction check at start-up or in the background. Ford is the main user: its engine and transmission modules compare a ROM checksum and set P0605 with the check engine light; the diesel transmission module tests once per trip at start.

causes.text: Program memory corrupted by an interrupted reflash
Internal flash or ROM defect
Faulty module software (update available)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module

symptoms: Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected

P0606.title: Control Module Processor
P0606.summary: P0606 means the module doubts the integrity of its own processor. Checks include a question-and-answer game between main and monitoring processor (GM: new seed via SPI within 450 ms; Ford: 'quizzer' level 3), arithmetic unit and register tests, stack overflow, the order in which safety-critical software runs, and the internal voltage supply (Ford diesel: 5 V rail outside 4.7–5.3 V).

causes.text: Faulty module software (update available)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Internal hardware defect (processor, voltage regulator, output stage chip)
Short on a 5 V sensor reference loading the internal supply

symptoms: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power or RPM limit
Often together with voltage codes P0562/P0563

P0607.title: Control Module Performance
P0607.summary: P0607 is the general 'module not working correctly' code, used when no specific memory or processor part is named. Ford sets it for wrong instruction execution or too many processor resets in engine and transmission modules; the Ford diesel after five communication errors with its monitoring chip within 20 s (a complete loss of that link is P0600).

causes.text: Faulty module software (update available)
Internal module defect (processor, clock, monitoring chip)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Electrical interference, e.g. from a faulty alternator or ignition

P0608.title: Control Module VSS Output A
P0608.summary: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0608 concerns output A: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an open circuit or an internal driver fault, as CARB requires for output components.

causes.text: Short or open in the output line A to the receiving module
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground
Internal driver fault in the module

P0609.title: Control Module VSS Output B
P0609.summary: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0609 concerns output B: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an open circuit or an internal driver fault, as CARB requires for output components.

causes.text: Short or open in the output line B to the receiving module
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground
Internal driver fault in the module

symptoms: Speed-dependent function of the receiver on output B disturbed
Cruise control or add-on device without speed signal

P060A.title: Internal Control Module Monitoring Processor Performance
P060A.summary: Electronic throttle systems use three levels: level 1 runs the engine, level 2 recalculates key values independently on the same processor, and level 3 is a separate monitoring processor that quizzes the main one and can shut down the throttle outputs. P060A means this monitoring processor (level 3) or its cooperation with the main processor is faulty: the question-and-answer game fails, an operating system call ends with an unrecoverable error, or the self-test of the monitoring module fails (Ford diesel: 5 s).

causes.text: Faulty module software (update available)
Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Internal hardware defect (monitoring processor, memory)
Moisture or corrosion in the module or connector

symptoms: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp

P060B.title: Internal Control Module A/D Processing Performance
P060B.summary: The analog-to-digital converter turns every analog sensor voltage into a number, so a faulty converter can falsify many values at once. The module checks it by timing its start-up calibration (GM 6.6 L diesel: 0.30 s or longer is a fault), by converting fixed internal reference voltages (about 4.73–4.83 V must be read), by grounding a test channel that must then read near 0 V (Ford diesel: over 249 mV is a fault) and by comparing with a second converter.

causes.text: Faulty module software (update available)
Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Internal defect of the converter or its chip
Shorted sensor input pulling the converter reference

symptoms: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Several sensor or misfire codes at the same time
ABS/ESC warning if the brake module set the code

P060C.title: Internal Control Module Main Processor Performance
P060C.summary: P060C reports a fault in the main processor that actually runs the engine, found either by the monitoring processor (Ford 'quizzer', level 3) or by duplicate storage and recalculation (GM). Typical findings are corrupted RAM or ROM data, arithmetic unit errors, memory address violations, a wrong program sequence or internal supply or temperature out of range (Ford diesel: internal voltage outside 1.3–3.3 V, 5 s).

causes.text: Faulty module software (update available)
Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Internal hardware defect (memory, processor)
Overheating or moisture in the module

symptoms: Driver assistance such as adaptive cruise unavailable
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected

P060D.title: Internal Control Module Accelerator Pedal Position Performance
P060D.summary: The accelerator pedal has two sensor tracks. With P060D the module's own cross-check of the pedal value fails: two processors (GM: main and 'motor' processor) calculate pedal position independently and must agree, and an active test briefly pulls one track to ground – the other must not follow, otherwise the tracks are shorted together.

causes.text: Short between the two pedal sensor signal lines or moisture in the pedal connector
Faulty pedal sensor (tracks drifting)
Faulty module software (update available)
Internal module fault (converter, processor)

symptoms: Reduced power, engine barely responds to the pedal
Check engine light or wrench lamp

P060E.title: Internal Control Module Throttle Position Performance
P060E.summary: P060E is the throttle counterpart of P060D. The throttle body also has two position sensor tracks, and the module checks whether it can still detect a short between them: during an active test one track is influenced briefly, and the second processor (GM 'motor processor') confirms that the test actually ran.

causes.text: Short between the throttle sensor signal lines or moisture in the throttle connector
Faulty throttle body (sensor)
Internal module fault (test circuit, second processor)
Faulty module software (update available)

symptoms: Check engine light (GM) or service lamp (GM Europe)

P060F.title: Internal Control Module Coolant Temperature Performance
P060F.summary: Coolant temperature feeds the torque model of the engine (friction, cold start), which the level 2 monitoring of the electronic throttle concept recalculates. P060F means the module's internal cross-check of this value failed: the temperature used by the main software and the value captured or recalculated by the monitoring level or a second converter path do not agree.

causes.text: Internal module fault in a converter or processor path
Faulty module software (update available)
Loose contact at the coolant temperature sensor that jumps between samples
Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)

symptoms: Check engine light or service lamp

P0610.title: Control Module Vehicle Options Error
P0610.summary: The module checks its vehicle-specific configuration for completeness and validity: at Ford the vehicle identification block or as-built data with tyre circumference, axle ratio, transmission and options; at GM the programmed vehicle options. Ford 2012 sets P0610 when one or more fields of that block are configured wrongly, the Ford diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s; GM and Saab V6 engines set it in the first trip, also for incomplete programming.

causes.text: Module not or wrongly configured after replacement (used part, missing as-built data)
Interrupted or faulty reprogramming
Changed tyre size or axle ratio without updating the data
Internal memory fault of the module

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on maker and variant)
Wrong speedometer reading or shift points
Optional functions such as cruise control missing

P0611.title: Fuel Injector Control Module Performance
P0611.summary: P0611 concerns systems with a separate injector control module or injector driver stage. On GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY the injector driver unit reports a microcontroller, monitoring or converter fault or a timeout to the engine module over CAN; the code sets after 30 of 50 checks at 125 ms with battery voltage of 10–18 V, and the lamp follows after two trips.

causes.text: Faulty voltage converter or driver stage in the injector module (Ford 6.0 L)
Low battery voltage, weak batteries or poor ground
CAN or supply line between engine and injector module disturbed
Faulty module software (update available)

symptoms: Hard or no start, especially when cold
Check engine light (GM after two trips)

P0612.title: Fuel Injector Control Module Relay Control
P0612.summary: Some diesels have a separate injector driver module that is powered through a relay switched by the engine module – GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY with its injector driver unit, Ford's 6.0 L Power Stroke with its injector control module. P0612 means the commanded relay state and the voltage measured back at the output do not match.

causes.text: Injector module relay faulty (coil open, contacts welded)
Relay control or feedback wire open or corroded, fuse
Low battery voltage or ground problems
Driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Engine does not start or stalls while driving
Check engine light (GM after two trips)
Battery drain if the relay does not drop out
Often together with P0611 or injector codes

P0613.title: TCM Processor
P0613.summary: P0613 reports an internal processor or calculation fault in the transmission control module. It is usually set by the transmission module itself – the scan tool shows which module stored it; on some architectures the engine module reports it on the transmission module's behalf.

causes.text: Transmission module software (self-diagnosis triggers falsely)
Voltage dip, poor ground or supply at the transmission module
Interrupted or faulty programming
Internal hardware defect (moisture, overheating)

symptoms: Check engine light or transmission warning
Transmission limp mode (fixed gear, harsh shifts)
Often no noticeable symptoms (sporadic false report)

P0614.title: ECM/TCM Incompatible
P0614.summary: P0614 means the software or calibration variant of the engine module does not match the fitted transmission module or transmission type, or the transmission module is not registered. CARB allows modules with several calibration variants (for example manual and automatic) to share one calibration ID only if a wrong variant turns on the lamp – exactly this check.

causes.text: Engine or transmission module replaced and not matched or registered
Used module with the wrong variant (different gearbox or engine)
Software update on only one of the two modules
Internal engine module fault

symptoms: Possibly transmission limp mode or limited shifting

P0615.title: Starter Relay A Circuit
P0615.summary: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits.

causes.text: Starter relay faulty (coil open)
Control wire open, harness chafed or pinched, connector corroded
Relay ground, fuse or supply faulty
Driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light only with some makers

P0616.title: Starter Relay A Circuit Low
P0616.summary: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits.

causes.text: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Relay coil shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in the relay or fuse box
Driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Possibly blown fuse in the relay circuit
Check engine light only with some makers

P0617.title: Starter Relay A Circuit High
P0617.summary: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits.

causes.text: Control wire shorted to a battery feed (harness damage)
Relay faulty internally (contact to coil, welded)
Voltage fed in by retrofitted electrics (remote start, alarm)
Driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Engine does not crank, or the starter keeps running
Check engine light only with some makers

P0618.title: Alternative Fuel Control Module KAM Error
P0618.summary: CARB treats gas-fuelled vehicles (CNG, LPG, also the gas mode of bi-fuel cars) like petrol cars up to model year 2018 and under an approved manufacturer plan afterwards. P0618 is meant for vehicles with a separate control module for the alternative fuel: it reports an error in that module's keep alive memory, which holds learned values while the ignition is off and loses them when power is cut – the gas counterpart of P0603.

causes.text: Power interruption at the gas module (battery disconnected, fuse, loose contact)
Poor supply, ground or corrosion at the module (underbody mounting)
Software or programming fault of the gas module
Internal memory defect

symptoms: Check engine or gas system warning light
Switch to petrol, gas mode blocked (bi-fuel)
Rough idle until values are relearned

P0619.title: Alternative Fuel Control Module RAM/ROM Error
P0619.summary: CARB treats gas-fuelled vehicles (CNG, LPG, also the gas mode of bi-fuel cars) like petrol cars up to model year 2018 and under an approved manufacturer plan afterwards. P0619 means the separate alternative fuel module reports an error in its working memory (RAM, read/write test) or program memory (ROM/flash, checksum) – one code for both, while the engine module uses P0604 and P0605.

causes.text: Interrupted or faulty programming of the gas module
Voltage dips, supply, ground or corrosion
Internal hardware defect (memory chip)
Manufacturer software fault

symptoms: Check engine or gas system warning light
No gas operation, switch to petrol
Starting problems on dedicated gas engines

P061A.title: Internal Control Module Torque Performance
P061A.summary: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061A is the result of the torque comparison: the commanded or estimated torque exceeds the permitted torque for the current operating point (Ford diesel 2023: within 0.1 s).

causes.text: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Contradictory inputs (pedal, throttle, air mass, cruise request) produce an implausible torque demand
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Internal defect of the engine module
Unapproved power upgrade (torque model no longer fits)

symptoms: Reduced power or limp mode, poor throttle response
Wrench, service or check engine lamp depending on the maker

P061B.title: Internal Control Module Torque Calculation Performance
P061B.summary: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061B means the torque calculation itself is inconsistent: main software and monitoring compute the torque differently.

causes.text: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Dirty throttle or air path, idle adaptation at its limit (petrol)
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Injector quantity deviation pushing the zero-fuel calibration out of range (diesel)
Internal defect of the engine module

symptoms: Check engine light and wrench lamp
Fluctuating idle (Ford petrol with dirty throttle)

P061C.title: Internal Control Module Engine RPM Performance
P061C.summary: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061C means the two internal engine speed calculations from the crankshaft signal disagree.

causes.text: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Disturbed crankshaft signal (sensor, reluctor, shielding, connector, interference)
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Internal defect of the engine module

symptoms: Check engine, wrench or service lamp
Stumbling or brief misfires with a disturbed signal

P061D.title: Internal Control Module Engine Air Mass Performance
P061D.summary: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061D means the independent recalculation of air mass or engine load disagrees with the main software's value.

causes.text: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Implausible air mass or load signal (dirty MAF, vacuum leak after the sensor)
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Dirty throttle, adaptation at its limit
Internal defect of the engine module

symptoms: Check engine and wrench lamp (Ford) or service lamp
Often air flow or mixture codes as well

P061E.title: Internal Control Module Brake Signal Performance
P061E.summary: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. Torque monitoring needs a reliable brake signal: brake applied means zero driver demand, cruise is cancelled, and in pedal limp mode the engine returns to idle.

causes.text: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Brake light switch misadjusted or faulty (both outputs do not switch together)
Faulty brake data from the ABS module or CAN disturbance
Connector or wiring fault at the brake switch
Internal defect of the engine module

symptoms: Wrench lamp (Ford), no check engine light

P061F.title: Internal Control Module Throttle Actuator Controller Performance
P061F.summary: P061F monitors the throttle position controller inside the engine module and its communication with the main processor. At Ford the main processor sends the target throttle angle to this controller (generation 2: a 312.5 Hz duty cycle signal, 10–92 % for 0–82°), which drives the throttle motor via an H-bridge; the monitoring checks that the target is implemented and reported back correctly.

causes.text: Internal fault in the throttle controller of the engine module
Throttle stiff, sooted or iced, controller at its limit
Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Throttle motor connector or wiring resistance
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module

symptoms: Wrench lamp (Ford), check engine light on generation 2
Throttle in default position, raised idle, barely any response

P0620.title: Generator Control Circuit
P0620.summary: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0620 is the general control circuit code.

causes.text: Connector or wire between module and alternator (corrosion, break, chafing)
Alternator or regulator faulty, including its LIN interface
Battery flat or faulty, jump start or charger connected
Loose or worn drive belt
Engine module or gateway (software, driver)

symptoms: Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems

P0621.title: Generator Lamp/L Terminal Circuit
P0621.summary: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0621 concerns the L line: the engine module applies voltage through a high-side driver and so switches the regulator's field control on and off.

causes.text: L line or alternator connector open or shorted
Regulator or alternator faulty
Ground problems between engine and body
Driver in the module faulty

symptoms: Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems
Starting problems after a longer drive

P0622.title: Generator Field/F Terminal Circuit
P0622.summary: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0622 checks the F feedback: its duty cycle equals the field on-time, from which the module calculates alternator torque and raises idle under load.

causes.text: F line or alternator connector open or shorted
Regulator or alternator faulty (field driver)
Alternator not charging (belt, brushes), duty cycle implausible
Module or software

symptoms: Check engine light possible on GM from model year 2023
Idle fluctuates or drops when large loads switch on
Flat battery with a real charging fault

P0623.title: Generator Lamp Control Circuit
P0623.summary: P0623 concerns the control of the battery warning lamp by a module's output driver, not the alternator itself. Traditionally the regulator switches the lamp through terminal L; where a module switches it instead – GM's Saab 9-4X turns the lamp on 15 s after a charging code – it can monitor its lamp output for open or short circuits.

causes.text: Wire or connector to the lamp or instrument cluster
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Output driver in the module
Ground fault

symptoms: Battery lamp never lights (not even at bulb check) or stays on
Real charging faults may not be displayed

P0624.title: Fuel Cap Lamp Control Circuit
P0624.summary: Despite its neighbours, P0624 has nothing to do with the alternator: it is the control circuit of the 'check fuel cap' warning lamp of the evaporative system. Ford's evaporative monitor lights such a lamp when, after refuelling, the tank cannot be pulled into vacuum – a gross leak or missing cap (P0457) – and turns it off once the cap is secured; not every vehicle has this lamp.

causes.text: Wire or connector to the warning lamp or instrument cluster
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Output driver in the engine or body module

symptoms: Fuel cap lamp never lights or stays on
A loose cap is no longer indicated

P0625.title: Generator Field/F Terminal Circuit Low
P0625.summary: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0625 means the F feedback is too low: with the engine running the regulator reports (almost) no field duty cycle – typically an open or grounded F line, or the alternator is not charging.

causes.text: F line open or shorted to ground, connector corroded
Regulator or alternator faulty or not charging (brushes, field winding)
Alternator B+ feed missing or high resistance
Engine module

symptoms: Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems
Check engine light on some Ford variants

P0626.title: Generator Field/F Terminal Circuit High
P0626.summary: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0626 means the F feedback is too high – a duty cycle near 100 % when little or no field current is expected, typically a short to battery voltage.

causes.text: F line shorted to battery voltage (chafing), connector
Regulator faulty (field permanently on, possibly overcharging)
Engine module software (Ram 6.7 L 2019)
Module input faulty

symptoms: Battery or check engine lamp (Chrysler/Ford partly with MIL)
Possibly overvoltage or overcharging with a regulator fault

P0627.title: Fuel Pump A Control Circuit/Open
P0627.summary: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump relay. P0627 is the open or general circuit fault.

causes.text: Fuel pump relay or pump driver module faulty
Wire or connector to relay or pump open or corroded (tank, underbody)
Fuel pump itself (winding open, overheated)
Fuse or ground point
Driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Engine does not start or stalls
Lack of power or stumbling under load
Pump not audible with ignition on

P0628.title: Fuel Pump A Control Circuit Low
P0628.summary: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump relay. P0628 means a short to ground: GM detects 0.5 Ω or less to ground with the driver on (8 of 10 samples at 250 ms; two trips in 2018, first trip in 2025); the driver then shuts off, the relay does not pull in and the pump stops.

causes.text: Control wire to relay or pump shorted to ground (chafing)
Relay coil shorted
Pump or pump module shorted internally (Ford high side)
Driver in the engine module faulty

P0629.title: Fuel Pump A Control Circuit High
P0629.summary: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump relay. P0629 means a short to battery voltage: GM detects voltage at the output while the driver is off (8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, two trips in 2018); because the driver hardware cannot always separate open circuit and short to voltage, P0627 may set as well.

causes.text: Control wire shorted to a battery feed
Relay contacts welded or relay faulty internally
Moisture in the relay or fuse box
Driver in the engine module shorted

symptoms: Pump runs constantly or after switch-off

P062A.title: Fuel Pump A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P062A.summary: P062A is a plausibility check of the fuel pump control circuit, not a plain short or open. On Ford's 2023 diesels (F-250 to F-550 and 3.0 L) the lift pump module reports its status as a duty cycle; outside 78–82 % – the expected 'good' signal – the code sets after 0.5 s.

causes.text: Pump driver module faulty or reporting an error status
Engine module software (false trigger)
Contact problems or resistance in signal or supply wires
Pump stiff or overloaded

P062B.title: Internal Control Module Fuel Injector Control Performance
P062B.summary: P062B monitors the injector driver stage inside the engine module. On direct injection engines a separate driver chip generates the boost voltage for opening the injectors and is configured by the main processor via SPI; GM checks initialisation, boost voltage (petrol: 90 V or more or 40 V or less), self-test, data download and communication, and sets the code in the first trip – while it is active, single injector circuit codes are suppressed.

causes.text: Short to ground on an injector high-voltage or control wire, or a faulty injector
Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Undervoltage or supply problem (battery, main relay)
Faulty driver chip in the engine module

symptoms: Check engine light (GM in the first trip)
Other injector codes are not reported while P062B is active (GM)

P062C.title: Internal Control Module Vehicle Speed Performance
P062C.summary: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. Vehicle speed feeds torque monitoring through cruise control, speed limiter and gear-dependent limits.

causes.text: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Disturbed vehicle or output speed signal (sensor, reluctor, ABS CAN data)
Wrong tyre size or axle ratio configured in the module
Internal defect of the engine module

symptoms: Wrench lamp (Ford), check engine light only on older Ford

P062D.title: Fuel Injector Driver Circuit Performance Bank 1
P062D.summary: Direct-injection injectors (petrol and common-rail diesel) need a high boost voltage generated in the module to open fast; the module then holds them with pulsed battery voltage. P062D monitors this boost voltage or the shared injector supply of bank 1.

causes.text: Short in an injector high-side wire or injector collapsing the boost voltage
Module internal (boost converter, driver chip)
System undervoltage or poor ground
Harness or injector connector (moisture, oil)

symptoms: Check engine light (GM in the first trip)
Loss of power or limp mode

P062E.title: Fuel Injector Driver Circuit Performance Bank 2
P062E.summary: Direct-injection injectors (petrol and common-rail diesel) need a high boost voltage generated in the module to open fast; the module then holds them with pulsed battery voltage. P062E is the bank 2 counterpart of P062D for V engines with separate driver circuits per bank.

causes.text: Short in an injector wire or injector of bank 2
Engine module or driver chip faulty internally
Connector or harness under the bank 2 valve cover
Undervoltage or poor ground

symptoms: Misfires on one side of the engine
Loss of power or limp mode

P062F.title: Internal Control Module EEPROM Error
P062F.summary: Learned values, adaptations, counters and configuration are saved to non-volatile memory (EEPROM or flash-emulated NVM) when the module shuts down. P062F means this memory failed a check: GM and GM Europe test at start-up whether the last write at shutdown completed, GM's 6.6 L diesel checks a checksum per data block and whether sectors can be erased, Ford's diesel reports read, write or erase errors (5 s).

causes.text: Shutdown interrupted (battery disconnected, voltage dip, main relay drops out too early)
Weak battery, poor ground or supply at the module
Software fault or incomplete programming
Memory defect in the module (write cycles, ageing)

symptoms: Check engine or service lamp (depending on the maker, sometimes after two trips)
Learned values lost: rough idle or harsh shifts until relearned

P0630.title: VIN Not Programmed or Incompatible ECM/PCM
P0630.summary: Since model year 2005 CARB requires exactly one module to report the VIN to a scan tool, and reprogramming the VIN must erase all emission-related diagnostic data. P0630 means the engine module holds no valid VIN or one that does not fit.

causes.text: New replacement module without written VIN
Used module from another vehicle (VIN does not match)
Interrupted programming or missing configuration data from the body module (Ford)
Internal memory fault

symptoms: Check engine light (some Ford trucks without)
Scan tool shows no or a wrong VIN
Ford: wrong tyre or axle data, speedometer errors

P0631.title: VIN Not Programmed or Incompatible TCM
P0631.summary: P0631 is the transmission module counterpart of P0630: the transmission control module holds no VIN, an invalid one, or one that does not match the vehicle – usually compared with the VIN of the engine or body module. Typical is a replaced transmission module or mechatronic unit (on dual-clutch and automatic gearboxes with integrated control) that was not VIN-programmed, or a used part.

causes.text: Transmission module or mechatronic unit replaced, VIN not written
Used transmission module from another vehicle
Interrupted transmission module programming
CAN communication fault during the VIN comparison

symptoms: Check engine light or transmission warning
Scan tool shows no or a wrong VIN in the transmission module

P0632.title: Odometer Not Programmed ECM/PCM
P0632.summary: Engine modules increasingly keep their own copy of the odometer reading or take it over from the instrument cluster or body module; for model years 2019–2021 onward CARB requires mileage in the module's operating data records and explicitly mentions the case 'odometer is lost'. P0632 means the engine module holds no valid odometer value.

causes.text: Engine module replaced, mileage not transferred
Several modules (engine, body, cluster) replaced or programmed at the same time
No communication to the cluster or body module during takeover
Internal memory fault (EEPROM/NVM)

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Scan tool shows no or a different mileage in the engine module
Implausible service or oil change displays

P0633.title: Immobilizer Key Not Programmed ECM/PCM
P0633.summary: The immobiliser couples the engine module to the immobiliser control module (GM body module, Chrysler SKIM/WCM) through a secret key and a challenge-response exchange – 'key' here means these security data, not the ignition key. P0633 means the engine module has not learned this secret key yet.

causes.text: Engine module replaced, immobiliser not learned
Learn procedure aborted or learn mode not exited (no start for another reason)
Communication fault to the immobiliser module
Engine module software fault (false setting)

symptoms: Engine does not start or dies immediately
Security or immobiliser lamp on or flashing
Code present after engine module replacement until learned

P0634.title: Control Module Internal Temperature A Too High
P0634.summary: The module measures its own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor and sets P0634 when it overheats. In practice this concerns mainly transmission modules mounted in or on the gearbox, such as GM's 6T70/6T75 and 6L units with the module in the valve body, surrounded by transmission fluid.

causes.text: Transmission fluid too hot: cooler clogged, lines kinked, air flow blocked, wrong level
Engine overheating
Charging system overvoltage (18 V or more)
Faulty internal temperature sensor or valve body module
High sustained load (towing, mountain driving, heat)

symptoms: Transmission limp mode (fixed gear), harsh shifts
Transmission warning, check engine light depending on the maker

P0635.title: Power Steering Control Circuit
P0635.summary: P0635–P0637 concern the control or signal circuit between engine module and power steering – depending on the maker the drive of an electro-hydraulic pump or the steering load signal the engine module uses to raise idle. CARB requires power steering components to be monitored only if another diagnostic uses them, so these codes are rare and maker-specific.

causes.text: Wire or connector between engine module and steering module or pump open or corroded
Software or calibration fault in the steering module (Mercedes)
Steering module or electro-hydraulic pump faulty
Undervoltage from weak battery, alternator or poor ground
Engine module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Fault possibly only after engine start

P0636.title: Power Steering Control Circuit Low
P0636.summary: P0635–P0637 concern the control or signal circuit between engine module and power steering – depending on the maker the drive of an electro-hydraulic pump or the steering load signal the engine module uses to raise idle. CARB requires power steering components to be monitored only if another diagnostic uses them, so these codes are rare and maker-specific.

causes.text: Signal or control wire shorted to ground (chafing)
Undervoltage from battery, alternator or ground
Steering module or pump module faulty internally
Engine module driver faulty

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)

P0637.title: Power Steering Control Circuit High
P0637.summary: P0635–P0637 concern the control or signal circuit between engine module and power steering – depending on the maker the drive of an electro-hydraulic pump or the steering load signal the engine module uses to raise idle. CARB requires power steering components to be monitored only if another diagnostic uses them, so these codes are rare and maker-specific.

causes.text: Control or signal wire shorted to battery voltage
Steering module or pump module faulty internally
Overvoltage from the alternator regulator
Engine module faulty

symptoms: Heavy steering or pump running constantly

P0638.title: Throttle Actuator Control Range/Performance Bank 1
P0638.summary: The electronic throttle motor positions the throttle plate; P0638 means the actuator does not follow its command on bank 1 (or the only throttle): target and actual angle from the two position sensors differ, or the motor needs too much duty cycle to hold the position. Subaru (also sold as Saab 9-2X) sets it at more than 3.5° deviation for 250 ms or over 95 % duty cycle for 2 s, lights the lamp at once and lets the spring set the plate to about 6° – raised idle, almost no power.

causes.text: Throttle dirty, sooted or stiff
Icing from condensation in frost
Throttle motor or gears worn
Resistance in the motor control wires
Module or software

symptoms: Check engine or electronic throttle light
Limp mode: much reduced power, raised idle
Often after a cold start in frost

P0639.title: Throttle Actuator Control Range/Performance Bank 2
P0639.summary: P0639 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0638 and only applies to engines with two separate electronic throttles, one per cylinder bank (some V8, V10 and V12 engines with separate intake paths). The module compares target and actual angle and the duty cycle the motor needs; if the plate does not follow, it is de-energised and springs to its rest position, and power is limited.

causes.text: Bank 2 throttle dirty or stiff
Bank 2 actuator motor or gears faulty
Icing
Wiring or module

symptoms: Rough idle from uneven bank filling

P063A.title: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A
P063A.summary: Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics.

causes.text: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded
Alternator or regulator faulty
Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds
Battery faulty

symptoms: Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery)

P063B.title: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A Range/Performance
P063B.summary: Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics.

causes.text: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded
Alternator or regulator faulty
Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds
Battery faulty

symptoms: Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery)

P063C.title: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A Low
P063C.summary: Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics.

causes.text: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded
Alternator or regulator faulty
Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds
Battery faulty

symptoms: Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery)

P063D.title: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A High
P063D.summary: Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics.

causes.text: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded
Alternator or regulator faulty
Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds
Battery faulty

symptoms: Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery)

P063E.title: Auto Configuration Throttle Input Not Present Bank 1
P063E.summary: Some modules configure themselves at start-up by detecting which inputs are present. P063E means the module expects a throttle position input for bank 1 but does not detect it.

causes.text: Throttle sensor or unit not connected, connector or wire open
Wrong module software or variant for the vehicle (module from another model)
Faulty throttle unit
Internal module fault

P063F.title: Auto Configuration Engine Coolant Temperature Input Not Present
P063F.summary: Some modules configure themselves at start-up by detecting which inputs are present. P063F means the module expects a coolant temperature input but does not detect it during this self-configuration.

causes.text: Coolant temperature sensor not connected, connector or wire open
Wrong module software or variant
Faulty sensor
Internal module fault

P0640.title: Intake Air Heater Control Circuit
P0640.summary: Some diesels (for example GM's 6.6 L Duramax LML and the Cummins in Ram trucks) warm the intake air with a heater grid switched by a relay or semiconductor switch. P0640 reports a fault in its control circuit.

causes.text: Heater relay or switching module faulty
Control wire or connector open or corroded
Heater grid burnt out or shorted to ground
Heater main cable or fuse loose or faulty
Glow plug or engine module faulty

symptoms: Poor cold start in low temperatures
White smoke, rough running after cold start
Flat battery if the relay sticks

P0641.title: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit/Open
P0641.summary: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time.

causes.text: Short to ground or voltage at one of the supplied sensors or its wire
A sensor signal wire shorted to voltage
Harness damage (chafing, rodent bite, water in connector)
Module internal (reference regulator)

symptoms: Many codes from several sensors at once

P0642.title: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit Low
P0642.summary: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time.

causes.text: 5 V wire or sensor shorted to ground
Internal short in a supplied sensor (e.g. pressure sensor)
Chafed harness or water ingress
Module reference regulator faulty

symptoms: Many codes from several sensors at once

P0643.title: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit High
P0643.summary: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time.

causes.text: 5 V wire shorted to battery voltage
Signal wire of a supplied sensor shorted to voltage
Sensor faulty internally
Module faulty

P0644.title: Driver Display Serial Communication Circuit
P0644.summary: P0644 concerns a dedicated serial line on which the engine module sends values or warnings to a driver display or information display – not the general vehicle CAN bus. The module reports missing or invalid communication on that line (open, short, display not answering); CARB requires digital outputs to be checked for communication faults.

causes.text: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Display or instrument cluster faulty or without supply (fuse, ground)
Low system voltage during cranking
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: Warning message or lamp (depending on the maker)
Information in the driver display missing, frozen or jumping

P0645.title: A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit
P0645.summary: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0645 is the general circuit fault of the relay coil control, usually an open circuit.

causes.text: A/C clutch relay faulty (coil open)
Control wire or connector open, terminals spread
Relay or clutch supply fuse blown (e.g. shorted clutch coil)
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: A/C not cooling (compressor does not engage)
Check engine light usually off, code stored only
Rarely no start if a shared fuse has blown (GM 3.4 L)

P0646.title: A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit Low
P0646.summary: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0646 means the voltage at the control output is too low while the driver is off – the control wire is shorted to ground, so the relay can pull in permanently and the compressor keeps running, which can ice up the evaporator.

causes.text: Control wire between relay and module shorted to ground (chafing)
Relay faulty internally (coil, ground)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: A/C compressor runs constantly, even with A/C off
With an open circuit: no cooling

P0647.title: A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit High
P0647.summary: The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0647 means the voltage at the control output stays too high while the driver switches on (it should pull to ground) – the control wire is shorted to voltage; the driver shuts off for protection and the relay does not pull in, so there is no cooling.

causes.text: Control wire shorted to a supply wire (chafing)
Relay with internal short (coil bypassed, very low resistance)
Wrong relay fitted
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: Code stored, check engine light usually off

P0648.title: Immobilizer Lamp Control Circuit
P0648.summary: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0648 concerns the immobiliser or security lamp where the engine module drives it directly by wire – on GM and Saab systems this lamp shows the immobiliser learn mode and faults.

causes.text: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Instrument cluster (board, connector) faulty
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: Immobiliser lamp off, permanently on or flashing wrongly

P0649.title: Speed Control Lamp Control Circuit
P0649.summary: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0649 concerns the cruise control ('speed control') indicator where the engine module drives it by wire.

causes.text: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Instrument cluster faulty
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: Cruise control indicator not working or stays on
Cruise control possibly disabled (depending on the maker)

P064A.title: Fuel Pump Control Module A
P064A.summary: Demand-controlled fuel systems drive the pump through a separate pump control module; the engine module sets the target and reads its status back. P064A means this module reports an internal fault.

causes.text: Pump control module faulty internally (output stage, electronics)
Output stage overheating from a stiff or worn pump or poor module cooling
Supply or ground fault or corrosion at the module (often on frame or tank)
Disturbed monitor line, so a wrong duty cycle is read

symptoms: Check engine light (GM) or stored code only (Ford petrol)
Hard start, stumbling or lack of power from low fuel pressure
Stalling or no start if the pump is switched off
Fuel pressure codes as well (e.g. P0087)

P064B.title: PTO Control Module
P064B.summary: A power take-off (PTO) drives equipment on trucks and pick-ups – tipper, crane, hydraulic pump or winch – from the engine or transmission. A PTO control module, or the PTO function in the engine module, manages switching, working speed and release conditions; P064B reports a fault of this module or an implausible PTO request.

causes.text: Engine or PTO module software or calibration (implausible torque or speed request)
PTO equipment installed or programmed incorrectly by the upfitter
Harness, connector or supply of the PTO module or switches
PTO control module faulty

symptoms: PTO switches off or cannot be engaged
Engine speed hunts with PTO active or stays below about 1100 rpm (Chrysler)
Warning lamp or stored code; driving usually normal

P064C.title: Glow Plug Control Module 1
P064C.summary: On diesels a glow plug control module switches the glow plugs (at Ford also the DEF heaters) with semiconductor switches, diagnoses itself and reports to the engine module. P064C means this module reports an internal fault.

causes.text: Glow plug module faulty internally (switches, memory)
Insufficient supply or ground (battery, corrosion, main fuse)
Short in a glow plug or wire overloading a driver
Moisture or corrosion in the connector of the engine-mounted module

symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in cold weather
White smoke and rough running after a cold start
Glow plug circuit codes as well

P064D.title: Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1
P064D.summary: Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064D means this chip for bank 1 sensor 1 does not work correctly or its messages are invalid.

causes.text: Engine module (lambda chip) faulty
Wiring or sensor fault pushing the chip into an invalid state (short to battery voltage, water in connector)
Faulty wide-band sensor (e.g. heater-to-signal short)
Voltage dips or software

symptoms: Higher fuel consumption, rough running (open loop)
Codes for the bank 1 sensor 1 wide-band sensor

P064E.title: Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 2
P064E.summary: Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064E is the bank 2 counterpart of P064D and only occurs on V and boxer engines with two sensors before the catalysts.

causes.text: Engine module (lambda chip bank 2) faulty
Wiring or connector fault of the bank 2 sensor 1
Bank 2 wide-band sensor faulty
Voltage dips or software

symptoms: Codes for the bank 2 sensor 1 wide-band sensor

P064F.title: Unauthorized Software/Calibration Detected
P064F.summary: P064F means the module has found that its software or calibration is not the version released by the manufacturer, or fails an authenticity check (signature, checksum, security keys). CARB requires manufacturers to protect calibrations against changes without special tools and to report calibration IDs and checksums.

causes.text: Unapproved or tuned software (chip tuning, programmer)
Faulty or interrupted reflash, outdated software
Used or replaced module without learning the security keys, wrong configuration
Module faulty internally (key storage)

symptoms: Check engine light (GM in the first trip)
Possibly follow-up codes in other modules or communication problems

P0650.title: MIL Control Circuit/Open
P0650.summary: The engine module switches the check engine light (MIL) through a low-side driver – or sends the command over CAN – and monitors the circuit: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V. CARB requires the MIL to light for a bulb check at ignition on with the engine off (at least 15 s since model year 2005).

causes.text: Wire or connector between engine module and instrument cluster open or corroded
MIL bulb burnt out or LED/instrument cluster faulty
MIL supply in the cluster missing (fuse, ignition feed)
Short in the circuit (at GM reported as P263A/P263B)
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: MIL does not light at the bulb check
MIL stays on (with a short or combined code)
Code only visible with a scan tool, engine runs normally

P0651.title: Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit/Open
P0651.summary: The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V.

causes.text: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor (camshaft, pedal, pressure)
Chafing or water in harness or connector
A sensor signal wire shorted to voltage
Module internal voltage regulator

symptoms: Several sensor codes at once (camshaft, pedal, pressure)

P0652.title: Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit Low
P0652.summary: The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V.

causes.text: 5 V reference wire shorted to ground (chafing)
Sensor on the reference circuit shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in a connector
Module

P0653.title: Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit High
P0653.summary: The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V.

causes.text: Reference or sensor signal wire shorted to a 12 V line
Faulty sensor feeding in external voltage
Module voltage regulator

symptoms: Implausible sensor values in live data

P0654.title: Engine RPM Output Circuit/Open
P0654.summary: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0654 concerns the engine speed output: the module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer and other modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle.

causes.text: Wire between module and tachometer or receiver open, connector corroded
Output wire shorted
Instrument cluster or receiving module faulty (input stage)
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: Functions using the speed signal disturbed (accessories, cruise control, shift indicator)
Check engine light depending on the maker

P0655.title: Engine Hot Lamp Output Control Circuit
P0655.summary: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0655 concerns the engine hot or coolant warning lamp that the engine module switches by wire from the coolant temperature signal.

causes.text: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Lamp supply missing (fuse)
Output driver in the module faulty

symptoms: Temperature warning lamp does not light at bulb check or when overheating
Warning lamp stays on without overheating
Code stored, check engine light depending on the maker

P0656.title: Fuel Level Output Circuit
P0656.summary: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. Where the engine module reads the fuel level sender itself – it needs the level for the evaporative leak test – it passes the level on to the fuel gauge.

causes.text: Wire or connector between module and instrument cluster open or shorted
Instrument cluster (fuel gauge input) faulty
Output driver in the module faulty
Fuel level sender fault as root cause

P0657.title: Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit/Open
P0657.summary: Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0657 is the open-circuit code; it is documented at Ford: the high-side switch of the 5R110W and 6R80 automatics feeds all shift solenoids, and the 2023 diesels split them into two supplies (P0657 and P2669), checked continuously.

causes.text: Open or connector fault at the transmission pass-through connector or wire to the valve body
Damaged harness
Internal high-side switch in the engine or transmission module
Internal transmission harness

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the variant)

P0658.title: Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit Low
P0658.summary: Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0658 means the supply output is too low with the driver on – a short to ground (0.5 Ω or less).

causes.text: Actuator supply wire shorted to ground
Actuator (solenoid) shorted internally
Transmission harness or connector (also open, in transmission modules)
Module internal (main cause on the Saab diesel)

symptoms: Transmission limp mode or fixed gear

P0659.title: Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit High
P0659.summary: Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0659 means a short to voltage on the supply output, checked with the driver off – the output should then be dead (GM: 0.5 Ω or less to the supply, 20 of 25 samples; lamp after two trips in 2017–18, none in 2016).

causes.text: Actuator supply wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Harness chafed against a 12 V line
Module (driver shorted; internal on the Saab diesel)
External voltage fed back through a faulty actuator

P065A.title: Generator System Performance
P065A.summary: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065A is the function check of the whole charging strategy.

causes.text: Electrical fault in another module (lighting, wipers, blower) disabling smart charging
Loose or corroded B+ or high-current connection
Engine module software
Alternator or regulator faulty

P065B.title: Generator A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P065B.summary: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065B is the plausibility check of the control channel to the alternator regulator (LIN or a dedicated smart-charge line): command and feedback do not match, or the signal is out of range (too low or too high).

causes.text: LIN or control wire between alternator and module (connector, corrosion, open)
Weak battery, jump start or external charging
Alternator regulator faulty
Ground or B+ connections

P065C.title: Generator A Mechanical Performance
P065C.summary: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065C points to the alternator's mechanical drive: the alternator does not deliver as commanded or its feedback does not match engine speed, typically because the belt slips.

causes.text: Drive belt slipping (tension, wear, oil)
Weak belt tensioner
Alternator overrunning pulley faulty
Alternator bearing or rotor stiff

P065D.title: Reductant System Malfunction Lamp Control Circuit
P065D.summary: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. On SCR diesels a separate lamp or symbol warns of low DEF/AdBlue level, poor quality or system faults and announces speed or start restrictions (inducement).

causes.text: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty
Lamp supply missing (fuse)
Driver in the engine or SCR module faulty

symptoms: AdBlue warning lamp does not light at ignition on, or stays on
No early warning of low AdBlue (risk of speed limit or no-restart without notice)
Check engine light possible (depending on the maker)

P065E.title: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Performance Bank 1
P065E.summary: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P065E is the function check for bank 1 (or the only valve): the valve does not follow its command.

causes.text: Valve shaft or linkage stiff or sooted (oil mist from crankcase ventilation or EGR)
Plastic lever or ball joint between actuator and shaft broken or detached
Actuator motor or solenoid faulty (weak, gears)
Manifold leak or, on vacuum-operated actuators, a leak in the vacuum line

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Torque gap in one rev band
Rattling or clicking from the intake manifold

P065F.title: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Performance Bank 2
P065F.summary: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P065F is the function check of the bank 2 valve: it does not follow its command, detected via a position sensor or the intake pressure pulsation (GM patent).

causes.text: Bank 2 valve or shaft sooted or stiff
Linkage between actuator and valve broken or unhooked
Bank 2 actuator faulty internally
Manifold or vacuum leak

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Torque gap in one rev band

P0660.title: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P0660.summary: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P0660 means the control circuit of the bank 1 (or only) valve is open.

causes.text: Actuator connector loose, corroded or spread
Actuator coil or motor open internally
Broken or chafed wire (control or supply)
Supply (fuse, main relay) to the actuator missing
Output driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light (GM after two trips; Ford without)
Less power in the upper or middle rev range
Actuator does not click at ignition on or when switching

P0661.title: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P0661.summary: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P0661 means the bank 1 control circuit voltage is too low with the driver off – a short to ground (0.5 Ω or less), which bypasses the driver and keeps the valve energised; GM also includes an open circuit (200 kΩ or more) here, so P0660 may set alongside.

Actuator shorted internally to housing or ground
Open circuit (connector, coil) – included under P0661 at GM
Output driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light after two trips (GM)
Torque or power gap in one rev band

P0662.title: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit High Bank 1
P0662.summary: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). Actuator winding shorted (very low resistance, overcurrent)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector between supply and control pin
Output driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Loss of power in part of the rev range
Actuator does not click when switching

P0663.title: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit/Open Bank 2

P0666.title: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit

Moisture or corrosion in the module or valve body

P066A.title: Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
P066A.summary: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named.

Rough running and white smoke right after a cold start

Module input faulty

P069E.title: Fuel Pump Control Module Requested MIL Illumination

Moisture or fluid in the module electronics
Module supply or software
